Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
News reports about events similar to what happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of witnessed other trauma, the appraisal that others can see what happened to me by looking at me is hard to reconcile unless there was also direct victimization or visible injury. The rest of the profile centers on witnessing, guilt about failing to protect, and anger that perpetrators were not held accountable, which fits. This item implies a conspicuous personal mark or shame signal not otherwise supported by the triggers, memory, or strategies, so it is clinically incoherent within this profile.

vignette:
Valentina Restrepo is a seventy-year-old Colombian-American fashion designer who presents with a PCL-5 score of 71, seeking help for symptoms she has carried, largely in silence, for several years. She is married, lives in Miami, and until recently maintained an active professional life designing resort wear - a career built around color, sensation, and the pleasure of fabric against skin. That last detail has become, for her, a source of dread she cannot fully explain to colleagues or to herself.

The event that fractured her sense of safety occurred during a visit to her extended family in Medellín. She was present when a close family member - her younger nephew - was struck by a vehicle during what had begun as an ordinary afternoon in a busy street market. The day was unseasonably warm, and she recalls the particular quality of the heat pressing against her arms and face in the moments before the impact. She had been distracted, browsing a textile stall, when she heard the sound. She reached him within seconds, knelt beside him on the hot pavement, and held him as emergency services were called. He survived, but with permanent injuries. Valentina has never been able to stop returning to those minutes on the street - the weight of the sun on her skin, the helplessness, the certainty that she had been looking the wrong way.

The memory does not wait for her permission. It forces itself into her awareness without warning, arriving with a completeness that is almost hallucinatory - she can feel the heat of the pavement through her knees, smell the exhaust, hear the crowd closing in. When the full sensory reliving takes hold, it is not a recollection but a return, and she emerges from it shaking and disoriented. What makes this especially difficult is that the triggers are woven into her daily life in ways she cannot always anticipate. Warmth on her skin - the Miami sun through a studio window, the heat of a steamer she uses to press fabric - can instantly collapse the distance between present and past, pulling the memory forward without any transition. Valentina has come to dread the act of working with her steamers in particular, a tool once central to her craft.

The memory, when it surfaces, does not arrive neutrally. It arrives already annotated with accusation. She had come to believe, with a conviction she found impossible to argue herself out of, that she should have been watching more carefully - that her distraction at the textile stall was the operative cause of what happened. She is also certain that the driver, who faced no legal consequences, has continued his life entirely undisturbed, and this perceived absence of accountability intensifies her sense that the harm was both preventable and unaddressed. These appraisals, in turn, keep her vigilant in ways that paradoxically increase her exposure: she monitors news for reports of similar accidents, and when she encounters them, the negative appraisals flare - confirming, in her mind, that the world remains dangerous and that she remains culpable for not doing more. That heightened state of self-reproach then lowers her threshold for re-experiencing, so that the next warm afternoon or the next headline finds her already primed.

In response to these triggers, Valentina has constructed a careful architecture of avoidance. She no longer watches news broadcasts, has removed herself from family group chats that might surface photographs or memories of her nephew before the accident, and has begun turning away from anything that carries the texture of grief - including, gradually, the warmth and celebration that her work once embodied. She has started pushing away positive emotions when they arise in her studio, finding them somehow dangerous, as though allowing pleasure would leave her unguarded. Over time, this avoidance has narrowed her world in ways her husband and junior colleagues have noticed: she has declined three international collections in the past two years, offering health as the reason. The avoidance brings short-term relief but sustains the cycle - by never allowing the triggers to resolve, she ensures they remain potent, and the memory remains unintegrated.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment in her studio last spring when she pressed a length of linen with a hand steamer and found herself on the floor of a Medellín street market, unable to move, for what her assistant told her was nearly four minutes. She came to therapy hoping, above all, to be able to work again - and terrified that what she has come to believe about herself may simply be true.
